article.overview: A robotic manipulator arm is a jointed mechanical arm that positions a tool, sensor or sample container at a target. On a lunar mission, such an arm can dig or scoop regolith, hold an instrument against soil or rock, or move a sample from one part of a spacecraft to another. Using an arm lets a lander or rover place an instrument precisely without moving the whole vehicle. Three flown lunar examples are described: the scoop-and-trench mechanism on NASA's Surveyor 3 (1967), the short robotic arm on China's Yutu rover (Chang'e 3, 2013), and the sampling arm on the Chang'e 5 lander (2020). These examples differ considerably in complexity and purpose and should not be treated as one standard design.
article.description: The category name 'robotic manipulator arm' covers a broad family of devices. At one end is a simple extendable scoop moved by a motor and used mainly for soil testing. At the other end is a multi-joint arm with an interchangeable or separable end effector that collects, processes and transfers samples. What these devices share is a sequence of motorised or mechanical links, a means of positioning an end effector, and some way of commanding and monitoring the motion from Earth or from an onboard controller. Because the sources reviewed describe different generations and purposes of hardware, this article reports each example separately and does not infer a common specification.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Lunar manipulator arms have served four main purposes in the sources reviewed. First, soil mechanics testing: the Surveyor 3 surface sampler was used to test how lunar soil responded to bearing, trenching and impact loads [1][2]. Second, close-contact instrument placement: the Yutu rover arm carried an Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) and placed it close to the surface to analyse soil composition [9][10]. Third, sample acquisition and transfer: the Chang'e 5 arm collected regolith and small rocks and passed the sample container to the ascent vehicle [4][5]. Fourth, engineering demonstration: early arms showed that robotic surface manipulation was feasible before more complex sampling systems were developed.
article.operating_principle: A manipulator arm consists of links connected by joints. Each joint is driven by a motor or actuator, and the position of the end effector is determined by the joint angles. A controller commands the joints to move the end effector along a planned path, and sensors or cameras confirm the result. Surveyor 3 used a motor-driven scoop on a pantograph-type arm that could be extended away from the spacecraft or retracted toward it; motors moved the arm in azimuth and elevation, and the scoop could also be dropped onto the surface under gravity and a spring [1][2]. Chang'e 3 (Yutu) used a short arm to position the APXS against the target surface, with an in-flight calibration against a basalt reference sample mounted on the rover [9]. Chang'e 5 used an arm with four degrees of freedom according to the eoPortal summary of pre-mission Chinese publications; its end effector included a scoop and could be separated from the arm so that it could be transferred to the ascent vehicle [4].
article.scientific_importance: A manipulator arm allows scientists to make measurements in direct contact with the surface. Remote sensing from orbit or from a lander's deck cannot reveal the same mechanical or compositional information as direct soil handling. The Surveyor 3 sampler provided some of the earliest in-situ data on how lunar soil behaves under mechanical loading [1][2]. The Chang'e 3 APXS results were reported as composition measurements of soil along the rim of a fresh crater, interpreted as a new type of mare basalt not previously sampled [7]. The Chang'e 5 arm contributed to the return of lunar samples to Earth [4][5].

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass, size or power requirement for a robotic manipulator arm. The values below describe specific flown examples. Where a value could not be confirmed from a primary or accessible source, the record says so. No table is given because the three examples differ in purpose, era and architecture and are not directly comparable.

examples.name: Surveyor 3 soil mechanics surface sampler
examples.type: Historical lunar surface digging and scooping mechanism (flown, 1967)
examples.status: Flown and operated on the Moon; Surveyor 3 landed on 20 April 1967 according to the NASA Technical Reports Server abstract [1].
examples.architecture: Motor-driven scoop on an extendable pantograph-type arm. Not a multi-joint manipulator in the modern sense.

test_counts_reported.conflict_note: Wikipedia reports 7 bearing, 4 trench and 13 impact tests [2]. Other secondary material reports different counts; unresolved.

examples.qualification: The 120 mm scoop length and 175 mm trench depth are stated in Wikipedia without a primary citation [2]. The approximately 1.5 m reach is reported in secondary summaries that cite Wikipedia and a Smithsonian object record [2][3]; it was not found in the primary JPL record accessed for this article [1]. Mass, power, lifetime and dimensions of the sampler assembly are not publicly specified in the sources checked.

examples.name: Chang'e 3 Yutu rover robotic arm
examples.type: Rover-mounted short robotic arm carrying the APXS (flown, 2013)
examples.status: Flown and operated on the Moon. The Chang'e 3 lander touched down on 14 December 2013 and the Yutu rover was released about 7 hours 24 minutes later, according to a secondary account reproducing the IHEP/CAS announcement [9].
examples.architecture: Short robotic arm on the rover. The APXS was reported as the only payload on the arm [9].
examples.arm_deployment: First APXS deployment reported about two days after landing, placing the instrument about two to three centimetres above the regolith [9].
examples.apxs_in_flight_calibration: APXS powered on 23 December 2013; in-flight calibration against a basalt sample mounted on the rover completed over five minutes [9].
examples.apxs_ground_verification_reported: Relative deviations for major-element abundances under 15 wt.% at 30 mm working distance and 30 min acquisition time [8]. These values describe the instrument configuration tested on the ground and are not properties of the arm.
examples.qualification: Joint count, arm length, mass and power of the arm were not verified. The degrees-of-freedom search returned no primary source. The landing and deployment timing come from a secondary blog reproducing an IHEP/CAS announcement [9].

examples.name: Chang'e 5 sampling robotic arm
examples.type: Four-degree-of-freedom sampling arm with separable scoop end effector (flown, 2020)
examples.status: Flown and operated on the Moon. The lander-ascender touched down near Mons Rümker on 1 December 2020 [4].
examples.architecture: Robotic arm with a scoop end effector; the end effector containing the samples can be separated from the arm for transfer to the ascent vehicle [4].
examples.degrees_of_freedom_basis: eoPortal attributes the four-degree-of-freedom description to information published in Chinese papers, i.e. pre-mission reporting [4]. A secondary search summary of Chang'e 5 coverage also reports four degrees of freedom [4][5].
examples.joints_basis: Springer ICIRA 2021 chapter reports four joints in total (shoulder yaw, shoulder pitch and elbow pitch share similar composition); only the search snippet was accessed [6].

surface_sampling_system_reported.samplers: Two samplers for loose and sticky regolith
surface_sampling_system_reported.near_field_cameras: Two cameras mounted on the arm beside the samplers
surface_sampling_system_reported.source: Hong Kong Polytechnic University description, read from search metadata and not in full [5]

examples.qualification: The four-degree-of-freedom and four-joint descriptions come from pre-mission reporting or a conference snippet. Arm mass, dimensions and power were not stated in the sources accessed. Sources differ on which component transferred the sample container to the ascender [4][5].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a manipulator arm. The Surveyor 3 scoop was reported at about 120 mm long with a pantograph reach of about 1.5 m (secondary figure). Chang'e 5 arm dimensions were not stated in the sources accessed. The Chang'e 3 arm dimensions were not verified. The three examples differ in architecture and are not directly comparable.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass was not publicly specified for the Surveyor 3 sampler assembly, the Chang'e 3 Yutu arm or the Chang'e 5 arm in the sources accessed. The 1,731 g figure refers to the total lunar samples returned by Chang'e 5 and is not the arm mass [4].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power values for the three arms were not publicly specified in the sources accessed. Each arm is driven by motors whose power budget is part of the host lander or rover's power system; no verified power figure is given here.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Any lunar manipulator must operate in vacuum, under strong thermal cycling between lunar day and night, in abrasive dust and under radiation exposure. Engineering control of temperature is therefore essential. A PolyU description of the Chang'e 5 surface sampling system reports a compact thermal arrangement intended to keep components cool [5]; the specific temperature limits are not verified. Joints, bearings and drives must tolerate dust contamination. The Surveyor 3 sampler was tested with bearing, trench and impact activity, indicating that its mechanism had to survive mechanical loads during soil handling [2]. Motion must be controlled so that the arm does not damage itself, disturb the host vehicle or misplace the instrument it carries. Power and data interface details for each arm are described only at a general level in the sources accessed.
article.limitations: A manipulator arm adds mass, complexity and failure modes to a lander or rover. Its reach and workspace are limited by link length and joint layout, so it cannot reach beyond its geometry unless the host vehicle moves. Dust and abrasive regolith can affect joints, seals, cameras and sample containers. Single-purpose devices such as the Surveyor sampler do not generalise to arms that handle samples or instruments with different geometry. Sampling arms require a reliable handover mechanism between the surface and the ascent vehicle, which adds interfaces that must be verified.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Manipulator arms were carried as part of landers or rovers. The transportation and deployment pattern depends on whether the arm is fixed to a lander, mounted on a rover or used to hand over samples to another vehicle. The three examples illustrate these configurations. For a surface payload, Earth integration typically includes mounting the arm to the host vehicle, routing power and data, and verifying thermal and mechanical interfaces before launch. The arm must survive launch loads, trans-lunar cruise, landing shock and surface deployment.
transportation_process: Integrate the arm (or sampler) with the lander or rover on Earth and verify its mounting, power, thermal and data interfaces.
Launch the spacecraft on a launch vehicle and perform trans-lunar transfer.

Land the lander on the surface. The Surveyor 3 sampler was part of the lander's surface payload [1]. The Chang'e 3 arm was carried on the Yutu rover, released from the lander about 7 hours after landing [9]. The Chang'e 5 arm was part of the lander and ascent system [4].
Deploy and operate the arm. The Chang'e 3 APXS was positioned about two days after landing [9].

For sample return, transfer the end effector or sample container to the ascent vehicle. eoPortal describes the separable end effector being transferred [4]; a PolyU-derived summary states that the samplers moved the container from the lander to the ascender, and one source says the robotic arm itself lifted the container [5]. This difference is unresolved.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surveyor 3: motor-driven extension and retraction of the pantograph arm, with the scoop able to be dropped onto the surface under gravity and a spring [2]. Chang'e 3: robotic arm on the rover positioning the APXS close to the surface [9]. Chang'e 5: robotic arm collecting regolith and small rocks, followed by transfer of the sample-containing end effector to the ascent vehicle [4]. Rover-mounted arms need stowage, release and traverse-compatible routing; sample-return arms need containment, sealing and handover to the ascent vehicle. Specific values for these interfaces are not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Surveyor 3 landed on 20 April 1967 [1]. Apollo 12 landed within walking distance of it on 19 November 1969, and the astronauts removed a scoop from the sampler, which was returned to Earth [2]. The Yutu rover carried the APXS on its arm after the Chang'e 3 landing in December 2013 [9]. Chang'e 5 landed on 1 December 2020 and returned a total of 1,731 grams of lunar samples [4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with a specific lander or rover cannot be assessed from the sources accessed. Mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, power and data interface details for a new arm would need to be compared with verified spacecraft specifications. No compatibility claim is made in this article.

article.historical_significance: The Surveyor 3 sampler is historically important because it provided early lunar soil-mechanics measurements and because its scoop was later retrieved and returned to Earth by the Apollo 12 crew in 1969 [1][2]. The Yutu arm demonstrated close-contact composition measurement on a rover [7][9]. The Chang'e 5 arm contributed to the return of lunar samples to Earth in 2020 [4][5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Primary documents were not fully accessed. The JPL primary report for Surveyor 3 (JPL-PD-125 / NASA-CR-106136) was read as an abstract only, so several sampler figures rest on Wikipedia. Surveyor 3 test counts conflict across secondary sources. The Yutu arm's joint count, length and mass were not found in an accessible source. The Chang'e 5 four-degree-of-freedom and four-joint descriptions come from pre-mission reporting or a conference snippet, and the arm's mass and dimensions were not found. Sources differ on which component transferred the Chang'e 5 sample container. Environmental and power values for the arms are not publicly specified in the sources accessed. No lander or rover compatibility is asserted.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue check: ID 267, name 'Robotic manipulator arm' and category 14 'Robotics, mobility and deployment technology' match lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.

Surveyor 3 sampler: the 120 mm scoop length and 175 mm trench depth are from Wikipedia without primary citation. The approximately 1.5 m pantograph reach is from secondary summaries and was not found in the primary JPL record accessed (ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19690074497, abstract only).
Surveyor 3 test counts conflict across secondary sources (Wikipedia: 7 bearing, 4 trench, 13 impact). Unresolved.
Surveyor 3 Smithsonian object record (si.edu) returned HTTP 403; metadata taken from search results only.

Chang'e 3 Yutu arm: degrees of freedom, length, mass and power not verified. Landing date (14 December 2013), rover release timing and APXS deployment and calibration timing come from a secondary blog reproducing an IHEP/CAS announcement; the SpaceRef source could not be fetched.
Chang'e 3 APXS ground-verification figures (15 wt.% deviation, 30 mm, 30 min) describe the instrument configuration, not the arm.

Chang'e 5 arm: four degrees of freedom is attributed to pre-mission Chinese papers via eoPortal and was not independently confirmed. Four joints come from a Springer ICIRA 2021 search snippet; full text not accessed.
Chang'e 5 arm mass, dimensions and power were not found in any accessed source.
Chang'e 5 sample transfer: sources conflict on whether the separable end effector, the samplers or the robotic arm itself transferred the sample container to the ascender.
Chang'e 5 total of 1,731 g is the mission's total lunar sample return from eoPortal; the split between arm-collected and drill-collected material is not given.

PolyU surface sampling system details (two samplers, two near-field cameras, sealing unit, thermal arrangement) were read from search metadata and not in full. The publication date 2020-12-08 is inferred from the URL path.

Images: all Wikimedia Commons image_url values were checked over HTTP (200, image/jpeg) but their Commons file pages were not read, so credit and licence are unverified and no public-domain status is asserted.
